title: Pradyumna Mishra
html:
A Brahmana of Orissa

Among the devotees of Nilachala whom Sri Chaitanya regarded as His own was the brahmana householder Pradyumna Mishra. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him Pradyumna Mishra, and in the story about him simply Mishra; Vrindavana Dasa calls him Sri Pradyumna Mishra; Murari Gupta, Srila Pradyumna Mishra; Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” “the Mishra named Pradyumna.” According to one reading of the “Charitamrita” he also bore the name Dasa; of this, more below.

He was born into a family of brahmanas in Utkala, that is, in Orissa. So writes Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, both in the “Anubhashya” on the “Charitamrita,” where he calls him an Oriya brahmana, a resident of Orissa, and in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” where he is twice named among those born in Utkala: together with Bhavananda Raya and his sons, Shikhi Mahiti, Kashi Mishra, Prataparudra and others (on CB, Adi 2.31), and in the account of him in particular (on Adi 14.2); and so too hold the biographies. According to other accounts he came from Shrihatta (Sylhet) and only later settled in Orissa for good.1 He was a householder (grihastha) of noble family and high standing, righteous and exemplary in his life. Yet when he spoke with the Lord he called himself “a fallen and sinful family man” and “a brahmana who lives on alms”: this is a Vaishnava's humility, not an account of his worldly affairs.

“Foremost among the Vaishnavas”

Krishnadasa Kaviraja counts Pradyumna Mishra among the branches of the tree whose root and trunk is Sri Chaitanya Himself:

“Then come Kashi Mishra, Pradyumna Mishra and Bhavananda Raya, whose company gave the Lord great joy.” (CC, Adi 10.131)

The Lord met him when He returned to Puri from His journey through South India: “He showed mercy to Kashi Mishra and met Pradyumna Mishra and others” (CC, Madhya 1.129). Kavi Karnapura in his mahakavya paints this first meeting thus: “A certain fortunate man of abundant merit, an ocean of good fortune, named Pradyumna Mishra, joyfully made the pair of Gaurachandra's lotus feet the guest of his eyes.” And from that one glance alone the Lord's mercy poured upon him: a stream of tears burst from his eyes, as from a rain cloud in the month of Shravana (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 13.70–71).

At that time Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya was presenting the Vaishnavas of Puri to the Lord. In Karnapura's drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” he says: “This is Pradyumna Mishra, this is Vishnudasa” (act 8). And in the “Charitamrita” Sarvabhauma introduces him thus:

“This is Pradyumna Mishra, foremost among the Vaishnavas. He is Jagannatha's chief cook and is known by the name Dasa.” (CC, Madhya 10.43)2

Vrindavana Dasa, listing the Lord's associates who were born in Orissa, puts him first:

“Among them were Pradyumna Mishra, love divine embodied, and the two great steadfast souls, Paramananda and Ramananda.” (CB, Antya 3.184)

Of the devotees of Nilachala who one after another recognized Sri Chaitanya as the Lord of their life, he writes:

“Sri Pradyumna Mishra was an ocean of love for Krishna; to him Sri Gaurasundara gave His own feet.” (CB, Antya 5.211)3

Thus the Lord gave him His feet: He took him under His shelter as His servant.

When Advaita Acharya and the Gaudiya devotees came from Bengal to Nilachala, the Lord went out with His associates to meet them. Among those who went with Him Vrindavana Dasa names “Sri Pradyumna Mishra, foremost in prema-bhakti” (CB, Antya 8.57);4 and Murari Gupta too, in his list of those who went out to meet them, remembers “Srila Pradyumna Mishra” (Murari Gupta's “Karcha,” 4.17.19).

Pradyumna Mishra welcomed the Lord also when He returned to Puri after going as far as Kanai Natashala on the way to Vrindavana:

“The delighted devotees came to meet Him, and the Lord embraced them all with love. Kashi Mishra, Ramananda, Pradyumna, Sarvabhauma, Vaninatha, Shikhi and all the other devotees came.” (CC, Madhya 16.253–254)5

And when the Lord came back from Vrindavana, at Narendra-sarovara He was again met by Kashi Mishra, Pradyumna Mishra, Damodara Pandita, Haridasa Thakura, Shankara Pandita and others (CC, Madhya 25.222).

The Entering of Gaurahari

Kavi Karnapura writes in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika”:

“The appearance (avirbhava) of Gaurahari was in Nakula Brahmachari; and His entering (avesha) is likewise to be known in the Mishra named Pradyumna.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 73–74)

Avesha is a special entering of the Lord's power into His devotee. The devotee does not thereby become God; he remains His servant, and through him the Lord reveals Himself as He wishes. The biographies take this verse as spoken of Pradyumna Mishra. But Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati applies it to another Pradyumna — Pradyumna Brahmachari, whom the Lord named Nrisimhananda.6

“The Life of Pradyumna Mishra”

Vrindavana Dasa opens one of the chapters of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” thus:

“Glory to the Lord, the very life of Sri Pradyumna Mishra! Glory to Him who became the treasure of the heart of Sri Paramananda Puri!” (CB, Adi 14.2)7

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Gaudiya-bhashya”: in this chapter the Lord, still living in Navadvipa as a householder, shows the exemplary conduct of a Vaishnava grihastha — He whom Pradyumna Mishra, the ideal householder, worshipped as his Deity.

Nobility, learning and a householder's righteous life are not yet the goal in themselves. The Lord wished all this to find its meaning in serving Hari and His devotees; for this He sent Pradyumna Mishra to Srila Ramananda Raya — not a brahmana by birth, but the finest teacher of bhakti-rasa, a Vaishnava acharya. Pradyumna Mishra heard him as a disciple and received the causeless mercy of the Lord. This is the subject of the fifth chapter of the Antya-lila of the “Charitamrita.”

The Story of Pradyumna Mishra

Listing the pastimes of the Lord's last years, Krishnadasa Kaviraja says:

“Telling Pradyumna Mishra of Ramananda's qualities, the Lord had him hear talks about Krishna from Ramananda.” (CC, Madhya 1.264)

And at the end of the book, recalling the contents of its chapters, he says that in the fifth chapter of the Antya-lila is “the Lord's mercy to Pradyumna Mishra, whom He sent to hear talks of Krishna from Ramananda Raya” (CC, Antya 20.110). The chapter itself tells it thus.

One day Pradyumna Mishra came to the Lord, bowed at His feet and humbly asked:

“Hear me, O Lord: I am a wretched, lowly householder. By what fortune have I obtained Your feet, so rarely attained? I wish to hear talks about Krishna. Be kind to me and tell me about Krishna.” (CC, Antya 5.5–6)

The Lord, Himself the source of all talk of Krishna, answered as though He had no right to speak of the confidential rasas:

“The Lord said, ‘I know nothing of talks about Krishna. Only Ramananda knows them, and I hear them from his lips. It is your good fortune that your mind longs to hear about Krishna. Go to Ramananda and hear from him.’” (CC, Antya 5.7–8)

And He added that whoever has awakened a taste for talks of Krishna is truly fortunate, for without that taste, as the “Bhagavatam” says, even the most flawless performance of duty is only wasted labour (CC, Antya 5.9–10; Bhag. 1.2.8). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains: the Lord only pretends to be ignorant. He sends Pradyumna Mishra, a brahmana by birth (shaukra, “by seed”), as a disciple to Ramananda, who was not a brahmana by birth but was the guru of all varnas and ashramas.

Mishra went to Ramananda Raya's home. There a servant offered him a seat and asked him to wait: the master was busy and would soon come out. Ramananda was in the garden, in a secluded place.8 He had written a drama in Sanskrit, the “Jagannatha-vallabha,” to be staged before Sri Jagannatha, and was now teaching its songs and dance to two young devadasis — maidens dedicated to the service of Jagannatha (in Orissa they are still called mahari). He taught them to convey in dance and acting the feelings of the gopis, the deep meaning of every song, so that the dance would become an offering to Jagannatha.

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains what this service was. The maidens were to play the principal gopis, and Ramananda saw in them those who are to be served (sevya-buddhi), and himself as a maidservant following them. Knowing himself in his spiritual form to be a maidservant of Srimati Radhika, he himself bathed and adorned the girl who played Her role and taught both of them songs and service. His mind and body remained unmoved through it all: “What one feels on touching wood or stone, Ramananda by nature feels on touching a young woman” (CC, Antya 5.19). This is no worldly affair and no example to imitate: such service is beyond the power even of great sages who have conquered their senses, and the Lord Himself will say of it, “Ramananda alone has this qualification.” While Ramananda served in this way, no one dared to interrupt him.

When the servant told him that Pradyumna Mishra had come, Ramananda at once hurried to his guest, bowed respectfully and humbly said:

“You have been here a long while, and no one told me. I have committed an offence at your feet. Your coming has purified my home. Command me — what shall I, your servant, do?” (CC, Antya 5.29–30)

Mishra replied that he had come only to see him and now felt that his heart had become purer (CC, Antya 5.31). The hour was already late, and, saying nothing more, Mishra took his leave and went home (CC, Antya 5.32).

The next day he came to the Lord, and the Lord inquired if he had been able to hear about Krishna from Ramananda. Mishra told Him what Ramananda Raya had been doing (CC, Antya 5.33–34).9

Then the Lord — the model of humility, who seeks no honour for Himself but honours others — began to glorify His devotee's love for Krishna as greater than His own:

“I am a sannyasi and consider Myself detached; yet, to say nothing of seeing a woman, if I merely hear a woman's name, My body and mind are disturbed. Who can remain steady on seeing a woman? Hear, all of you, about Ramananda Raya — an account so wondrous that it can hardly be told. First, they are devadasis, maidservants of the Deity, and moreover they are beautiful young women; yet he himself performs every service for them. <…> Yet the mind of Raya Ramananda remains unmoved as he teaches them to express the stirrings of many different bhavas. His body and mind are unmoved, like wood or stone. How wonderful — at the touch of a young woman his mind is unmoved! Ramananda alone has this qualification; from it I know that his body is transcendental.” (CC, Antya 5.35–38, 40–42)

The nature of such a mind, the Lord went on, is known to Ramananda alone; but from the effect one may judge the cause. Whoever hears with faith of Krishna's rasa dance with the maidens of Vraja is freed from lust, the disease of the heart, and attains pure love (Bhag. 10.33.39). A mind established in pure goodness beyond the gunas is untouched by the mundane; and one who serves Krishna in love day and night is an eternally perfect soul. Therefore Ramananda's body is not of matter — it is made of consciousness and bliss, and so this great devotee (maha-bhagavata) is fit to speak of Krishna:

“I know that Raya's worship follows the path of raganuga. His body is like a perfected spiritual body (siddha-deha), and so his mind is not mundane.” (CC, Antya 5.51)

And the Lord sent Mishra to Ramananda once more:

“I too hear about Krishna from Raya. If you wish to hear, go there again. Tell him in My name: ‘He has sent me to hear about Krishna from you.’ Go quickly, while he is still in the hall.” (CC, Antya 5.52–54)

Mishra went at once. Ramananda received him with obeisances and asked what he could do for him; hearing that the Lord Himself had sent his guest, he counted it his great fortune: “Where else could I find such great fortune?” (CC, Antya 5.55–58). He took Mishra to a secluded room and asked what he wished to hear.

Mishra asked him to tell, in order, all that Ramananda had once spoken of with the Lord at Vidyanagara in the south — sambandha, abhidheya and prayojana: the soul's relationship with Krishna, the path to Him, and the goal, divine love. And he added:

“You are the instructor not only of others but of the Lord Himself! I am a poor mendicant brahmana, and you are my sustainer. I do not know how to ask anything, good or bad. Seeing how wretched I am, be merciful and tell me of your own accord.” (CC, Antya 5.61–62)

Ramananda began to speak of Krishna in due order, as he had once spoken to the Lord Himself, and in his words the nectar-ocean of rasa surged up (CC, Antya 5.63).

He himself raised the questions and himself answered them. The hour of the midday meal passed, and still the talk did not end; speaker and listener, absorbed in love for Krishna, forgot themselves and did not notice that the whole day had gone by. Only when the servant reminded them that the sun was setting did Ramananda fall silent (CC, Antya 5.64–66).

With deep respect he bade his guest farewell, and Mishra, as he left, cried, “My life is fulfilled!” and began to dance. At home he bathed, took prasada, and in the evening came to the Lord (CC, Antya 5.67–68).

His desire fulfilled, he bowed at the Lord's feet in great joy and told of his good fortune:

“Mishra said, ‘O Lord, You have fulfilled my life! You have plunged me into the nectar-ocean of talks about Krishna. The words of Ramananda Raya cannot be retold. Raya is not a mere human being; he is made of the rasa of devotion to Krishna.’” (CC, Antya 5.70–71)

On this verse Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes that to see a mortal man in a guru who sings of Krishna is forbidden. Mishra also passed on to the Lord the words of Ramananda himself: “Gaurachandra Himself speaks these words through my mouth. As He makes me speak, so I speak, like a vina” (CC, Antya 5.73) — and concluded:

“You have made me drink such rasa; birth after birth I have sold myself at Your feet.” (CC, Antya 5.76)

The Lord answered with fresh praise of Ramananda's humility: great souls never glorify themselves and ascribe their own words to others (CC, Antya 5.77–78).

Why the Lord Sent Mishra to Ramananda

Kaviraja himself explains the meaning of this pastime:

“Though a householder, Raya is not under the control of the six enemies (shad-varga); though seemingly a worldly man (vishayi), he instructs sannyasis. To reveal all these qualities of his, the Lord sent Mishra there to hear. <…> To destroy the pride of the sannyasis and panditas, He reveals dharma through a lowly shudra. He speaks of bhakti, prema and the truth (tattva), making Raya the speaker, while He Himself, together with Pradyumna Mishra, becomes the listener.” (CC, Antya 5.80–81, 84–85)

And at the close of the chapter Kaviraja names its subject once more: “Thus I have told the account of Pradyumna Mishra, who by the Lord's order heard talks about Krishna” — and within it he spoke of the glory of Ramananda, the full extent of which the Lord Himself described (CC, Antya 5.159–160).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in the “Anubhashya.” To the worldly eye Ramananda seemed a householder on the path of worldly action, a man absorbed in mundane affairs (vishayi). But his mind, established in pure goodness, always worshipped the pastimes of Krishna: he is “vishayi” only in the sense that his whole world is Krishna, and he is able to turn to Krishna even sannyasis who have renounced the world and seek the impersonal. In the world a brahmana is the teacher of the remaining three varnas, while a sannyasi is the teacher of brahmanas in the remaining three ashramas. To crush their pride in their position, the Lord, through the mouth of Ramananda, whom the world knew as a “shudra” and a “grihastha,” instructed Pradyumna Mishra, a brahmana by birth, and Himself, a sannyasi, accepted the dharma that Ramananda preached.

So the Lord, wishing to reveal to the world Ramananda's spiritual nature and greatness, showed his power to all through Pradyumna Mishra. And the lesson of this pastime is plain: neither worldly varna, nor ashrama, nor learning gives the right to teach true dharma; he teaches in whom there is love for Krishna. The pride of brahmana and sannyasi in their position is crushed when a brahmana by birth and the Lord Himself in the robes of a sannyasi humbly listen to one whom the world takes for a “shudra” and a householder.

In the Memory of the Vaishnavas

The “Vaishnava-vandanas” also preserve Pradyumna Mishra's name. Devakinandana Dasa writes: “I glorify Sri Pradyumna Mishra and Raya Bhavananda” (66);10 the “Vaishnavabhidhana” names him too (36).

Nothing more is known of his life. Neither the original sources nor the biographies speak of his years, or of when and where he left this world; nor are his days of appearance and disappearance found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Significance

Pradyumna Mishra entered the “Charitamrita” above all as a listener. He did not judge Ramananda by externals: Ramananda's service to the devadasis was performed in the spiritual body of a maidservant of Sri Radha, and the Lord, hearing of it, did not condemn but glorified him, revealing that his body is not mundane. Mishra himself teaches a disciple's humility: he goes to the one the Lord pointed out, calls himself fallen, does not presume to choose his own questions and asks to be told “in order,” and having heard, gives his heart to the Lord's feet and returns to Him to tell of the mercy received. A noble Oriya brahmana, “foremost among the Vaishnavas,” “foremost in prema-bhakti,” he showed how high position in the world finds its meaning when it bows before a Vaishnava.

Notes

  1. So writes the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana” of Haridasa Dasa, and the biographies after it; elsewhere one of them says plainly that he was born in Sylhet, and another calls him “a resident of Shrihatta.” The original sources say nothing of Shrihatta: Vrindavana Dasa names him among the associates “who took birth in Orissa” (CB, Antya 3.183–184). We follow Srila Bhaktisiddhanta. One of the biographies, passing on the “Gaudiya-bhashya,” specifies “in central Orissa”; in our translation of the commentary it says simply “in Orissa.” He may have been confused here with a namesake — Pradyumna Mishra of Shrihatta, to whom the Sanskrit “Sri Krishna-chaitanyodayavali,” with the Lord's genealogy, is ascribed (the authenticity of this work is disputed: it is held to be a late forgery); but this is only a supposition.
  2. The Bengali verse has “this” (iha) twice: “This is Pradyumna Mishra, foremost among the Vaishnavas; this is Jagannatha's chief cook, named Dasa.” It can also be understood as speaking of two different people. So it is in Karnapura, from whom Kaviraja takes this passage: in the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” Sarvabhauma separately presents to the Lord “the one called Dasa Mahasoar, in charge of the kitchen,” and separately, further on, Pradyumna Mishra. The biographies read the verse as speaking of one man. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that a brahmana may add “dasa” to his name as a sign that he is a servant of Vishnu; one of the biographies explains it otherwise — that “Dasa” is sometimes a family name of brahmana families in Orissa, though in Bengal it is borne by lower castes.
  3. In the Bengali, atma-pada yanre dila — “to whom He gave His own feet.” One of the biographies renders these words as though the Lord raised Pradyumna Mishra to His own level; this is wrong: the Lord gave him the shelter of His feet, and the devotee remains His servant. Some editions read the first line krishna-sukhera sagara, “an ocean of Krishna's happiness”; our edition has krishna-premera sagara, “an ocean of love for Krishna.”
  4. In one of the biographies and in one place in the “Anubhashya” this chapter of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” is called the ninth: evidently the chapters are divided differently in different editions. Another biography understands the verse as naming three as chief among the loving devotees of Puri — Kashishvara, Bhagavan Acharya and Pradyumna Mishra; but in the verse he alone is called “foremost” (pradhana).
  5. The verse has simply “Pradyumna”; one of the biographies takes it as Pradyumna Mishra.
  6. So in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.35, where this verse is cited in connection with Pradyumna Brahmachari; so too in the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” which calls the Brahmachari “an avesha of Gaura.” Elsewhere (on Adi 10.56) Srila Bhaktisiddhanta speaks of the appearance and the entering in Nakula Brahmachari and Pradyumna Mishra. The “Charitamrita” itself speaks of the Lord's entering into Nakula Brahmachari and of His appearance before Nrisimhananda, that is, Pradyumna Brahmachari (Antya 2). The biographies do not mention this in their account of Pradyumna Mishra.
  7. In the Gaudiya Math editions, Adi 13.2.
  8. One of the biographies calls it the Jagannatha-vallabha garden; the “Charitamrita” says only “into the garden.” The name of the garden may have been confused here with the name of the drama.
  9. According to the “Charitamrita,” Mishra came to the Lord the next day; one of the biographies says, after several days. The biographies also write that doubts about Ramananda's conduct arose in Mishra's mind, but they tell it differently in different places: according to one account, he at first kept silent because of them, but the Lord, who knows all hearts, understood his thoughts; according to another, he told everything and confessed his doubts; according to a third, after waiting long and hearing the servant, he lost his trust in Ramananda. The “Charitamrita” says nothing of doubts: Mishra told Ramananda that his heart had been purified, left because of the late hour, and the next day simply told the Lord what Raya had been doing. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  10. According to Majumdar, this couplet is not found in the old manuscripts.
